Pluralism (Ecclesiastical)
PLOO-ruh-liz-um
n. (the holding of two or more church benefices at once by one man, with the duties of all but one discharged by a deputy or not at all)
From Latin pluralis, of more than one; the ecclesiastical sense is distinct from the modern philosophical and religious senses of the word.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ecclesiastical pluralism is the holding of several livings at once. A man might be rector of three parishes, prebendary of a cathedral and archdeacon besides, drawing the income of all and residing in none, with curates paid a pittance to do the work. It was the standing abuse of the English church from the thirteenth century until the reforms of the eighteen-thirties, and it was repeatedly condemned by councils, repeatedly dispensed by popes and bishops, and never stopped until Parliament stopped it. The Lord settled the question of divided service in a sentence that is about money and is exactly applicable here: “No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24). And the shepherd whose own the sheep are not behaves predictably when anything costs him: “he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines pluralist as a clerk or clergyman who holds more ecclesiastical benefices than one with cure of souls; and plurality as the holding of two or more benefices by the same clergyman.

expand to see more

PLURALIST, n. A clerk or clergyman who holds more ecclesiastical benefices than one, with cure of souls.

PLURALITY, n. In the church of England, a plurality of benefices, where the same clergyman holds two or more.

DISPENSATION, n. The granting of a license, or the license itself, to do what is forbidden by laws or canons.

NON-RESIDENCE, n. The omission of residence on a benefice; the neglect of residing where official duties require.

CURE, n. Spiritual charge; the care of souls; the oversight of a parish.

Key Scripture

Mat 6:24 — "No man can serve two masters: for either he will hate the one, and love the other; or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other. Ye cannot serve God and mammon."

Joh 10:12 — "But he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd, whose own the sheep are not, seeth the wolf coming, and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth: and the wolf catcheth them, and scattereth the sheep."

Joh 10:13 — "The hireling fleeth, because he is an hireling, and careth not for the sheep."

Eze 34:4 — "The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken, neither have ye brought again that which was driven away, neither have ye sought that which was lost; but with force and with cruelty have ye ruled them."

Modern Corruption

One man holding three livings and residing in none, the standing abuse of the English church for six centuries.

expand to see more

The corruption is total and was always known to be. Every council that condemned pluralism was attended by pluralists; every dispensation that permitted it was granted by an authority that had condemned it; and the men who benefited were often sincerely devout. That is what makes it instructive. A system can be understood by everyone to be wrong and continue for six hundred years because the alternative costs the people who would have to change it.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that a cure of souls is a cure of particular souls who can be named. Ezekiel's charge against the shepherds is a list of omissions — “The diseased have ye not strengthened, neither have ye healed that which was sick, neither have ye bound up that which was broken” (Eze 34:4) — and omissions are what a man in another county necessarily commits. The hireling is defined not by taking wages but by what he does when the wolf comes, since he “careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin pluralis, more than one; Greek douleuo (G1398), to serve as a slave; Greek mamonas (G3126), mammon or wealth; Greek misthotos (G3411), a hireling; Hebrew chalah (H2470), to be sick.

expand to see more

Latin pluralis — of more than one; the ecclesiastical sense is a term of art.

Greek douleuo (G1398) — to serve as a bondman; “No man can serve two masters” (Mat 6:24).

Greek mamonas (G3126) — wealth personified; “Ye cannot serve God and mammon” (Mat 6:24).

Greek misthotos (G3411) — a hired man; “he that is an hireling, and not the shepherd” (Joh 10:12).

Greek melo (G3199) — to care for; “careth not for the sheep” (Joh 10:13).

Usage

"“or else he will hold to the one, and despise the other” (Mat 6:24) — the arithmetic of three livings."

"“and leaveth the sheep, and fleeth” (Joh 10:12) — what the deputy system produces."

"“neither have ye bound up that which was broken” (Eze 34:4) — omission, the absentee's sin."
